lead: Every polymer chain is built by one of two routes. In chain growth, an initiator creates a reactive centre and monomer units add to it one at a time; the chain stays alive until it dies. In step growth, any two molecules that carry the right groups can join, so dimers, trimers and long chains all react with one another. Industry picks the route from the monomer: PVC, polystyrene and polyethylene come from chain growth, PET bottles and nylon come from step growth. This chapter follows both mechanisms step by step.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for monomer, repeat unit and functionality; see Unit 3, Reaction kinetics, for rate ideas if a question asks for kinetics.

blocks.text: An addition monomer carries a double bond, C=C, or a ring. A condensation monomer carries two reactive groups, such as –COOH and –OH. That one difference decides everything else.

Addition is usually the same as chain growth, and condensation is usually the same as step growth, but not always — polyurethane is step growth without any condensation, so decide the mechanism from the monomer and the chemistry, not from the label.

items: Small molecule: chain growth releases nothing, so every monomer atom enters the chain. Step growth usually releases a small molecule — water from a diacid plus a diol, HCl from a diacid chloride plus a diamine. Polyurethane is an exception: diisocyanate plus diol releases nothing.

Molar mass: in chain growth the first chains reach full length within seconds, and extra monomer only makes more chains. In step growth every species grows together, so the degree of polymerisation stays small until almost all groups have reacted.

Monomers: chain growth needs one monomer with unsaturation plus a trace of initiator. Step growth needs two bifunctional monomers weighed in matched amounts, or one monomer carrying two different groups.

blocks.text: Because of the second point, the two routes need different reactor times. A chain-growth run can be stopped as soon as the monomer is used up; a step-growth run must be pushed to the very end, often under vacuum, or the product is a sticky oligomer.

sections.h3: Free-radical chain growth, step by step

blocks.text: Most addition polymers — polyethylene, PVC, polystyrene, poly(methyl methacrylate) — are made with free radicals. Four steps repeat millions of times.

items: Initiation. A peroxide or an azo compound splits on heating: I–I → 2 I•. The dot marks an unpaired electron, that is, a radical. The radical adds to one monomer: I• + CH₂=CHX → I–CH₂–CH•X. Here X is the side group — H for ethene, Cl for vinyl chloride, C₆H₅ for styrene, COOCH₃ for methyl methacrylate.

Propagation. The new radical attacks another monomer and the radical moves to the far end: ~CH₂–CH•X + CH₂=CHX → ~CH₂–CHX–CH₂–CH•X. The tilde ~ stands for the rest of the chain. Units add head to tail, so the backbone reads –CH₂–CHX–CH₂–CHX–.
Termination by combination. Two radicals join into one dead chain: ~CH₂–CH•X + •CHX–CH₂~ → ~CH₂–CHX–CHX–CH₂~.
Termination by disproportionation. One radical pulls a hydrogen atom from the other. Two dead chains form, one ending in a double bond: ~CH₂–CH•X + •CHX–CH₂~ → ~CH₂–CH₂X + CHX=CH~.

Chain transfer. A radical abstracts an atom from solvent, monomer or another chain, giving a dead chain and a new small radical: ~CH₂–CH•X + HS–R → ~CH₂–CH₂X + •S–R. Molar mass falls, but the overall rate barely changes.

blocks.text: The chain length is fixed at the instant of termination, which is why the molar mass of a free-radical polymer depends on how fast termination competes with propagation.

Cationic. A proton acid opens the double bond of an electron-rich monomer. Boron trifluoride with a trace of water, or sulphuric acid, is the usual initiator. The growing end is a carbocation such as ~C⁺(CH₃)₂, and polyisobutylene, the base of butyl rubber, is made this way. Styrene also polymerises cationically.

Anionic. An organolithium compound or sodium naphthalenide starts an anion, ~CH₂–CH⁻X. Styrene and butadiene polymerise cleanly in hexane with butyllithium. The chains stay alive while monomer remains, so the process is called living and gives a narrow spread of chain lengths.

Ring-opening. A cyclic monomer opens its ring and joins the chain end. Caprolactam gives nylon-6; ethylene oxide gives poly(ethylene glycol). No atom is lost, but the ring has opened, so the repeat unit is an open chain and not the ring-shaped monomer. Coordination routes with a transition metal catalyst are covered in 5.4.

sections.h3: Step growth: functionality two or more

blocks.text: A step-growth monomer must carry at least two functional groups. A molecule with only one group caps a chain and acts as an impurity. Two monomers of type A–A and B–B, or one monomer of type A–B, give a linear chain.

blocks.where: X̄ₙ is the number-average degree of polymerisation (monomer units per chain); p is the extent of reaction, the fraction of functional groups that have reacted, between 0 and 1.

blocks.text: The relation assumes equal numbers of A and B groups. Put p = 0.90 and X̄ₙ is 10; p = 0.99 gives 100; p = 0.999 gives 1000. A fibre or a bottle resin therefore needs conversion above 0.99, which is why PET and nylon reactors are driven hard, often under vacuum, to strip out water and push p upward.

A small imbalance between A and B groups caps the chain length, so the two monomers are weighed carefully. Networks need some monomer with three groups; that is discussed with structure and properties in 5.5.

figure.caption: Free-radical chain growth: the initiator makes the first radical, monomer units add one at a time during propagation, and two radicals meeting ends the chain. Notice that the chain length is fixed at the moment of termination.

spec.title: Free-radical chain growth
spec.aria: A top-to-bottom flow from monomer through initiation and propagation to termination, ending in a dead polymer chain.

examples.question: 1.00 mol of ethene is polymerised in the presence of 2.00 mmol of benzoyl peroxide, (C₆H₅CO)₂O₂. Each peroxide molecule breaks into two radicals, and each radical starts one chain (initiator efficiency taken as 1). (a) If termination is entirely by disproportionation, find the number of polymer chains and the number-average degree of polymerisation. (b) Repeat the calculation for termination by combination. Take N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
steps: Moles of initiator: n_I = 2.00 mmol = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol.
Initiator molecules = n_I × N_A = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.2044 × 10²¹ molecules.
Benzoyl peroxide splits as (C₆H₅CO)₂O₂ → 2 C₆H₅COO•, so each molecule gives two radicals. Radicals = 2 × 1.2044 × 10²¹ = 2.4088 × 10²¹ radicals.
(a) Disproportionation gives one dead chain per radical, so chains = 2.4088 × 10²¹.
(b) Combination joins two radicals into one chain, so chains = 2.4088 × 10²¹ ÷ 2 = 1.2044 × 10²¹.
examples.answer: (a) 2.4088 × 10²¹ chains with number-average DP 250; (b) 1.2044 × 10²¹ chains with DP 500.
examples.check:
NA = 6.022e23
n_monomer = 1.00
n_init = 2.00e-3
radicals = 2 * n_init * NA
print(radicals)
chains_disprop = radicals
dp_disprop = (n_monomer * NA) / chains_disprop
print(round(dp_disprop, 6))
chains_comb = chains_disprop / 2
print(chains_comb)
dp_comb = (n_monomer * NA) / chains_comb
print(round(dp_comb, 6))

traps: Condensation does not always release water. Diisocyanate plus diol, the polyurethane route, releases nothing at all. Decide from the monomer, not from the chapter heading.

Ring-opening polymerisation keeps every atom, but the ring has opened, so the repeat unit is an open chain and not the ring-shaped monomer. Caprolactam, C₆H₁₁NO, gives the repeat unit –[NH–(CH₂)₅–CO]–.
Chain transfer lowers molar mass without lowering the rate much. It does not stop polymerisation; it moves the radical onto a new molecule, which then carries on growing.
Termination by combination halves the number of chains and doubles DP compared with disproportionation. Mixing the two inside one DP calculation is the commonest slip.
High conversion alone does not give high molar mass in step growth: the A and B groups must also be balanced. The relation X̄ₙ = 1 ÷ (1 − p) assumes exact stoichiometry.

quiz.q: Which structural feature decides that a monomer can polymerise by chain growth?
quiz.a: A double bond C=C, or a ring that can be opened. That is the site where the initiator acts.

quiz.q: Why does a condensation polymer reach high molar mass only near complete conversion?
quiz.a: Any two molecules can react, so all chains grow together and stay short. DP = 1 ÷ (1 − p) rises steeply only as p approaches 1.

quiz.q: 0.500 mol of styrene is polymerised with 1.00 mmol of initiator, one radical per initiator molecule, termination by combination. Find the number of chains and the number-average DP. N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
A polyester sample reaches extent of reaction p = 0.98. Find its number-average DP.
A free-radical polymerisation is run in a solvent that is a good chain-transfer agent. Predict the effect on rate and on molar mass.
quiz.a: Rate stays nearly the same, because a radical is destroyed and a new one is created in the same step. Molar mass falls sharply, because chains are killed early and the new radicals start fresh short chains.

quiz.q: Write the propagation step for the free-radical polymerisation of vinyl chloride, CH₂=CHCl.
quiz.a: ~CH₂–CH•Cl + CH₂=CHCl → ~CH₂–CHCl–CH₂–CH•Cl. The radical moves to the far end and the repeat unit is –CH₂–CHCl–.

quiz.q: A condensation polymer sample has number-average DP 20. Estimate p and say why the sample feels weak and brittle.
quiz.a: X̄ₙ = 1 ÷ (1 − p) = 20, so 1 − p = 0.05 and p = 0.95. Short chains mean few entanglements and poor load transfer, so the material has low strength; a useful resin needs p above 0.99.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry rarely uses plain free radicals where control matters: reversible-deactivation methods such as ATRP and RAFT keep most chains alive, so all chains reach nearly the same length and block copolymers become possible. Living anionic polymerisation makes the thermoplastic elastomer SBS, used in shoe soles and in bitumen modification. Emulsion and suspension processes are how PVC and polystyrene actually leave a factory, because they carry the heat of polymerisation away in water. Search ATRP, RAFT, living polymerisation and the Carothers equation for the next step.
